title: Lesson 2: Relating the Standard & Vertex Forms: Completing the Square

source_refs.md_gate: MD PASS prepare — A2.8 NEW; A2.11 NEW scoped light; A2.7 REVIEW only

central_question: If someone hands you only the expanded equation of a curve that rises and then falls (or the other way around), how do you rewrite it so the high or low point is obvious — without guessing from a graph?
intended_understanding: Completing the square rewrites a quadratic from standard form f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c into vertex form f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k so the vertex (h, k) and related features become readable; the rewrite does not move the graph. Students use a diagram or tiles and matching algebra (including factoring out a when a ≠ 1, and simple rational b/a), verify equivalence with graphing technology, then sketch key features from standard via that path. Expanding (Lesson 1) and completing the square are inverse same-curve rewrites.
prerequisite_assumptions: Students can inspect vertex form for vertex, axis, and maximum or minimum, including plus-inside (x + …) as (x − h), and decide max vs min from the sign of a (Module 4 Lesson 1; A2.10 vertex share).

Students can expand f(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k into standard form and verify with graphing technology that the two writings are equivalent (Module 4 Lesson 1; A2.7). This lesson revisits that direction as review on a shared model; it does not new-teach expansion.
Roles of a, h, and k as transformations of y = x^2 are already taught (Module 1; A2.5). This lesson does not reteach stretching, reflecting, or sliding.
Students can already sketch g(x) = a(x − h)^2 + k from y = x^2 (Module 1; A2.6) once vertex form is in hand.
Students can expand and simplify quadratic expressions, including binomial squares (Module 2; A1.2). Completing the square undoes that fluency; expand skill is assumed, not retaught.

Students already inspect standard and factored form for intercepts and related features (Module 3; A2.10 share). This lesson does not reteach intercept reading; it may use factored form only as a light strategy alternative for sketching when friendly.
processes_to_teach: complete-square-diagram: Given a = 1 and integer b, complete the square with algebra tiles or an area diagram so the completed square and leftover constant are visible before any algebra.
complete-square-algebraic (a=1): Algebraically complete the square for f(x) = x^2 + bx + c (a = 1), matching the diagram steps, to produce f(x) = (x − h)^2 + k.
complete-square-factor-a: When a ≠ 1, factor a out of the x^2 and x terms before completing the square, then finish to a(x − h)^2 + k — treat forgetting to factor a as a dedicated fracture point.
complete-square-rational-b-over-a: Complete the square when b/a is a simple rational (Ministry e.g. ½, 0.75), as deliberate variation after integer cases.
verify-equivalence-tech: After producing vertex form, verify with graphing technology that standard and vertex writings are equivalent representations of the same curve.

sketch-from-standard-via-cts (A2.11 light): From a standard-form equation, complete the square to obtain the vertex (and axis / max-min from the produced vertex form), then sketch those key features — not the full interval / feature laundry list.

strategy-choose-cts-vs-factor (light): Given standard form, choose a suitable sketch strategy — completing the square for the vertex, or factoring when intercepts are friendly — with criteria, without teaching factoring as primary solving.

revisit L1 expand↔CTS on one shared model: On one quadratic written both ways, reverse Lesson 1’s expand path with completing the square and confirm both directions leave the graph unchanged (A2.7 review only).

purpose_map.purpose: Put students in a situation where they need the high or low point but are handed only standard form — so guessing from a graph is unavailable or unreliable.
Flip Lesson 1’s three-form contrast: given standard form of a familiar model, ask which writing would make the vertex readable, without yet completing the square. (Analyze: which form affords what.)

purpose_map.section: action: L1 revisit expand↔CTS on shared model
purpose_map.purpose: On one shared quadratic, show expand (vertex→standard) beside completing the square (standard→vertex); students confirm both rewrites leave the graph unchanged. Cognitive target Analyze; A2.7 review only — not new teach.
Fully demonstrate completing the square with tiles/diagram for a = 1, integer b, so the completed square and leftover are visible. Cognitive target Understand. (complete-square-diagram)
Match algebraic steps to the diagram on the same example, producing (x − h)^2 + k. Cognitive target Apply. (complete-square-algebraic)
Repeat algebraic completing the square on a second a = 1 case that varies the sign of b or c, so the first example is not a template to copy. (Apply)
Isolate factoring out a before completing when a ≠ 1; treat forgetting this step as the named fracture. Cognitive target Apply. (complete-square-factor-a)
Deliberate variation with simple rational b/a (e.g. ½, 0.75 per Ministry). Cognitive target Apply. (complete-square-rational-b-over-a)
Students verify that their completed-square vertex form and the original standard form share the same graph/table under graphing technology. Cognitive target Apply. (verify-equivalence-tech)

From standard form, CTS → read vertex, axis, max/min from the produced vertex form → sketch those key features only (A2.11 light; no full interval dump). Cognitive target Apply. (sketch-from-standard-via-cts)

On a short pair of standard-form equations, choose CTS vs factoring for sketching with stated criteria; plant when to wait for formula without teaching formula. Cognitive target Analyze. (strategy-choose-cts-vs-factor)
Return to the hook situation with a fresh standard-form model: complete the square independently, read max/min, sketch key features, and retrieve that completing the square does not move the curve.

hook_constraint: Need a situation where the high or low point matters but students are given only standard form (or an expanded model), so they cannot rely on an already-visible vertex equation. Prefer continuity with Lesson 1’s hook family if that situation can flip to standard-given; otherwise a new same-class context (path, throw, fountain, height). Consolidation must return to that same situation. No required login, Gizmos, or Desmos API. No Nelson CTS stems.
instructional_sequence_intent: Need high/low but only standard form given (hook) → which writing would show the vertex (minds-on flip) → shared-model L1 revisit expand↔CTS (same curve both ways) → worked diagram CTS (a=1) → matching algebraic CTS → varied a=1 → factor-out a ≠ 1 → rational b/a → tech verify equivalence → sketch key features from standard via CTS (A2.11 light) → light CTS-vs-factor strategy choice (plant formula) → consolidation returns to hook with Key Idea / Need to Know.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students think completing the square produces a different parabola rather than an equivalent representation of the same curve.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: When a ≠ 1, students complete the square on ax^2 + bx as if a were 1, or they factor a from only one term, so the inside of the square is wrong.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students take half of b with the wrong sign, or add (b/2)^2 without balancing, so h or k is off even when a = 1.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students stall or invent integer shortcuts when b/a is a simple rational (e.g. ½, 0.75), treating those cases as a different method instead of the same steps with fractions.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: After producing vertex form, students misread (x + …) as a positive h, repeating Lesson 1’s h-sign error on their own rewrite.

misconceptions.label: instructional_hypothesis
misconceptions.hypothesis: Students pick completing the square or factoring at random, or wait for a formula on every standard-form sketch, without criteria for which writing makes the needed feature readable.
